entries.18:13: The border continued south past Bethel and down toward the mountain south of lower Beth-horon. It's more detail fixing the shape of Benjamin's territory.
entries.18:14: The western border curved around from the mountain south of Beth-horon to Kiriath-jearim, a town belonging to Judah. It marks the edge of Benjamin's land on the west.
entries.18:15: The southern border started from the far side of Kiriath-jearim and ran out to the spring called Nephtoah. It's another boundary line defining the tribe's land.
entries.18:16: The line dropped down past the valley of Hinnom, along the Jebusite hill on the south, as far as En-rogel. It traces the southern edge in detail.
entries.18:17: The border went on past En-shemesh and Geliloth, opposite the road up to Adummim, down to the stone of Bohan. It keeps marking the outline of the territory.
entries.18:18: It continued along the slope facing the Arabah on the north and down into the Arabah valley. It's part of the same boundary description.
entries.18:19: The border ran to the north side of Beth-hoglah and ended at the northern tip of the Salt Sea where the Jordan empties in. That was Benjamin's southern limit.
entries.18:20: The Jordan River formed Benjamin's eastern border. This verse sums up that the whole territory was marked out on every side for their families.
entries.18:21: This begins a list of the towns belonging to Benjamin's families, starting with Jericho, Beth-hoglah, and Emek-kezziz. It shows the actual places the tribe would live in.
entries.18:22: The list continues with Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, and Bethel. These were towns within Benjamin's allotted land.
entries.18:23: The towns of Avvim, Parah, and Ophrah are added to Benjamin's list. It's a record of the places they received.
entries.18:24: Chephar-Ammoni, Ophni, and Geba are listed, making twelve towns plus their surrounding villages. It shows the tribe's holdings were concrete and counted.
entries.18:25: Gibeon, Ramah, and Beeroth are named next among Benjamin's towns. The list keeps track of each place they were given.
entries.18:26: Mizpeh, Chephirah, and Mozah are added to the list. These were more towns in Benjamin's territory.
entries.18:27: Rekem, Irpeel, and Taralah are named. The record continues town by town.
entries.18:28: The list ends with Zela, Eleph, the Jebusite city (Jerusalem), Gibeath, and Kiriath, making fourteen towns with their villages. This closes the account of Benjamin's inheritance by family groups.
entries.19:1: Simeon's share of the land was assigned second, and it sat inside the territory already given to Judah. This shows that God's promise to give each tribe land was being carried out in an orderly way.
entries.19:2: This begins a list of the towns that belonged to Simeon's tribe. The reader sees that their inheritance was made up of real, named places, not just a vague promise.
entries.19:3: More towns in Simeon's territory are named here. Each name shows the land was carefully divided and recorded for the families who would live there.
entries.19:4: The list of Simeon's towns continues. These details remind the reader that God's gift of land was specific and concrete.
entries.19:5: Simeon's towns keep being listed, including Ziklag. The careful record shows the tribe's inheritance was real and accounted for.
entries.19:6: This verse totals the towns so far and notes the villages around them. It shows the inheritance included both towns and the farmland and settlements nearby.
entries.19:7: Four more towns are added to Simeon's list, along with their surrounding villages. The reader sees the full extent of what the tribe received.
entries.19:8: This wraps up Simeon's territory, including the villages around the towns. It confirms that the whole inheritance was settled and complete.
entries.19:9: Simeon's land came out of Judah's larger portion because Judah had more than they needed. This shows generosity and cooperation between tribes rather than selfishness.
entries.19:10: Zebulun's share was assigned third, and its boundary started at a place called Sarid. The reader sees the land being divided tribe by tribe, just as planned.
entries.19:11: This describes the western edge of Zebulun's land, running past several landmarks. The boundaries were marked out clearly so everyone knew what belonged to them.
entries.19:12: The boundary line turns east and passes through several towns. These details show the land was measured and defined with care.
entries.19:13: The border continues eastward through more towns to its endpoint. The reader sees that Zebulun's territory was a specific, bounded area.
entries.19:14: The line curves around on the north side and ends at a valley. This completes the picture of Zebulun's borders.
entries.19:15: Five towns are named, with a total of twelve towns plus their villages. The list shows the inheritance was substantial and well recorded.
entries.19:16: This summarizes Zebulun's inheritance as these towns and their surrounding villages. It confirms the tribe's share was fully assigned.
entries.19:17: Issachar's share was assigned fourth, given to their families. The reader sees each tribe receiving its own place in turn.
entries.19:18: This starts the list of towns within Issachar's territory. The names show the land was real and specific.
entries.19:19: More towns in Issachar's area are named. The careful listing shows the inheritance was recorded for the families who would live there.
entries.19:20: The list of Issachar's towns continues. Each name marks part of the land God gave them.
entries.19:21: Four more towns are added to Issachar's territory. The reader sees the tribe's inheritance taking shape town by town.
entries.19:22: This describes the boundary reaching the Jordan River and totals sixteen towns with their villages. It shows Issachar's land was clearly defined and complete.
entries.19:23: This summarizes Issachar's inheritance as these towns and villages. It confirms their share was fully settled.
entries.19:24: Asher's share was assigned fifth, given to their families. The division of the land continues in an orderly way.
entries.19:25: This begins listing the towns in Asher's territory. The names show the land was concrete and carefully recorded.
entries.19:26: The boundary stretches to Mount Carmel on the west. This shows Asher's land reached the coast and included valuable areas.
entries.19:27: The border turns east and passes through several places, reaching as far as Cabul. The reader sees the land was measured out with clear landmarks.
entries.19:28: More towns are named, extending as far as the great city of Sidon. This shows Asher's territory reached into the northern region.
entries.19:29: The boundary loops around to Tyre and ends at the sea. This confirms Asher's land included a stretch of coastline.
entries.19:30: Three more towns are named, with a total of twenty-two towns plus their villages. The list shows the inheritance was sizable and complete.
entries.19:31: This summarizes Asher's inheritance as these towns and villages. It confirms their share was fully assigned.
entries.19:32: Naphtali's share was assigned sixth, given to their families. The land division continues tribe by tribe.
entries.19:33: This describes Naphtali's boundary starting from a large tree and running to the Jordan. The reader sees the land was marked out with clear landmarks.
entries.19:34: The border turns west and touches the lands of Zebulun, Asher, and Judah. This shows Naphtali's territory bordered several other tribes.
entries.19:35: This begins listing the fortified towns in Naphtali's territory. The names show the land included strong, defensible cities.
entries.19:36: More towns in Naphtali's area are named, including Hazor. The careful record shows the inheritance was real and specific.
entries.19:37: Three more towns are added to Naphtali's list. Each name marks part of the land given to the tribe.
entries.19:38: This ends the list with a total of nineteen towns plus their villages. It shows Naphtali's inheritance was fully recorded.
entries.19:39: This summarizes Naphtali's inheritance as these towns and villages. It confirms their share was completely settled.
entries.19:40: Dan's share was assigned seventh, given to their families. The reader sees the last of these tribes receiving its land.
entries.19:41: This verse starts listing the towns that marked the border of the land given to the tribe of Dan. It reminds the reader that God's gift of land was specific and real, not vague.
entries.19:42: This continues the list of towns in Dan's territory. Each name shows that the land was carefully divided and assigned, town by town.
entries.19:43: More towns are named as part of Dan's inheritance. The reader sees that the allocation was detailed and orderly.
entries.19:44: The list of Dan's towns keeps going. These names show that the land was actually handed over to real families and places.
entries.19:45: The verse adds more towns to Dan's share of the land. It shows the territory was made up of many small communities.
entries.19:46: This describes the western edge of Dan's land, near the sea opposite Joppa. It shows the territory had clear boundaries on the coast.
entries.19:47: Dan's land was too small for them, so they attacked the city of Leshem, destroyed its people, and settled there, renaming it after their ancestor Dan. It shows that even a promised gift sometimes needed effort and courage to fully take hold.
entries.19:48: This sums up Dan's inheritance as all these towns and their surrounding villages. It confirms that the whole tribe received a complete share of land.
entries.19:49: With the land divided among the tribes, the people also gave Joshua a share of his own. It shows that the leader was not forgotten but was honored by those he led.
entries.19:50: As the Lord directed, Joshua received the town he asked for, rebuilt it, and settled there. It shows that God's instructions were followed and that Joshua was rewarded for his faithful leadership.
entries.19:51: This closes the account of dividing the land, done by the priest, Joshua, and tribal leaders at Shiloh before the Lord. It shows the whole process was carried out under God's direction and was now finished.
entries.20:1: God is speaking directly to Joshua, the leader who took over after Moses. This shows that God was still guiding his people through their leader.
entries.20:2: God tells Joshua to set aside special towns as safe places, just as he had already instructed through Moses. God keeps his earlier promises and plans.
entries.20:3: These towns were for someone who killed another person by accident, not on purpose. The person could run there and be protected from the family member seeking revenge.
entries.20:4: When the person arrived, they would explain their case to the town leaders at the entrance area. If accepted, the leaders gave them a place to stay and kept them safe.
entries.20:5: If the relative seeking revenge chased after them, the town leaders were not allowed to hand the person over, because the death was accidental and not done out of hatred.
entries.20:6: The person had to stay in that safe town until a public trial was held and until the current high priest died. After that, they could go back home safely.
entries.20:7: The people chose three safe towns west of the Jordan River: Kedesh, Shechem, and Hebron. These were spread across the land so help was never too far away.
entries.20:8: They also chose three safe towns east of the Jordan: Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan. This made sure people on both sides of the river had a place to run to.
entries.20:9: These towns were open to Israelites and to foreigners living among them, so anyone who killed someone by accident could find protection and get a fair hearing before being judged.
entries.21:1: The leaders of the priestly tribe came to the top leaders of Israel to ask for what they had been promised. It shows that God's people were expected to follow through on commitments made to those who serve him.
entries.21:2: They reminded the leaders that God had commanded through Moses that they should receive towns to live in, along with pasture land for their animals. It means God's instructions included practical care for those who served him.
entries.21:3: The Israelites gave the Levites towns and pasture land out of the land they had received. It shows that sharing what God gives us with those who serve the community is part of obeying him.
entries.21:4: The first share went to the priestly families descended from Aaron, who received thirteen towns from three tribes. It means those with the most sacred duties were provided for first.
entries.21:5: The remaining families descended from Kohath received ten towns from three other tribes. It shows the distribution was organized fairly among the different family groups.
entries.21:6: The families descended from Gershon received thirteen towns from four tribes. It means each group got what it needed, spread across different parts of the land.
entries.21:7: The families descended from Merari received twelve towns from three tribes. It shows that even the smaller groups were not forgotten in the plan.
entries.21:8: The Israelites gave all these towns and pasture lands to the Levites, just as God had commanded through Moses. It means the whole arrangement was carried out in obedience to God.
entries.21:9: The list begins with towns taken from the tribes of Judah and Simeon. It shows the record was kept carefully so everyone could see what was given.
entries.21:10: These first towns went to the families of Aaron among the Kohathites, because they were first in line. It means priority was given to those with the highest priestly role.
entries.21:11: They received Hebron, an important town in the hill country of Judah, along with its pasture land. It means a significant and historic place was set apart for the priests.
entries.21:12: The fields and villages around the town itself went to Caleb as his own property. It shows that the priests got the town while Caleb kept the surrounding land, so both were provided for.
entries.21:13: Aaron's descendants received Hebron, a city of refuge, and Libnah, each with pasture land. It means the priests were given places of both safety and daily provision.
entries.21:14: Jattir and Eshtemoa were also given to them with their pasture land. It shows the gifts were specific and practical, not just general promises.
entries.21:15: Holon and Debir were included with their pasture land. It means the list continues to show real, usable places being handed over.
entries.21:16: Ain, Juttah, and Beth-shemesh were added, making nine towns from those two tribes. It shows the count was kept exact so nothing was left unclear.
entries.21:17: From Benjamin's tribe they received Gibeon and Geba with their pasture land. It means the provision came from several tribes working together.
entries.21:18: Anathoth and Almon were also given, making four towns from Benjamin. It shows even small groups of towns were carefully recorded.
entries.21:19: In total, Aaron's descendants received thirteen towns with their pasture land. It means the promise made to the priests was fully kept.
entries.21:20: The remaining Kohathite families received towns from the tribe of Ephraim. It shows the distribution continued in an orderly way for the other priestly families.
entries.21:21: They received Shechem, a city of refuge in the hill country of Ephraim, and Gezer, with their pasture land. It means they were given both a place of safety and land for their needs.
entries.21:22: Kibzaim and Beth-horon were added, making four towns. It shows the count was completed for that group.
entries.21:23: From Dan's tribe they received Elteke and Gibbethon with their pasture land. It means provision came from yet another part of the land.
entries.21:24: Aijalon and Gath-rimmon were also given, making four towns from Dan. It shows the gifts were spread out and carefully counted.
entries.21:25: From the half-tribe of Manasseh they received Taanach and Gath-rimmon with their pasture land. It means even the smaller tribal shares contributed to the Levites' support.
entries.21:26: All together, the remaining Kohathite families received ten towns with their pasture land. It means their total share matched what had been planned.
entries.21:27: The Gershonite families received Golan, a city of refuge in Bashan, and Ashtaroth, with their pasture land. It shows they too were given places of safety and provision.
entries.21:28: From Issachar's tribe they received Kishion and Daberath with their pasture land. It means the distribution continued tribe by tribe.
entries.21:29: Jarmuth and En-gannim were added, making four towns from Issachar. It shows the record kept an exact count for each group.
entries.21:30: From Asher's tribe they received Mishal and Abdon with their pasture land. It means more towns were handed over as promised.
entries.21:31: Helkath and Rehob were also given, making four towns from Asher. It shows the pattern of fair provision continued.
entries.21:32: From Naphtali they received Kedesh, a city of refuge in Galilee, along with Hammoth-dor and Kartan. It means they were given safety and land in the northern part of the country.
entries.21:33: In total, the Gershonite families received thirteen towns with their pasture land. It means their full share was completed as planned.
entries.21:34: The remaining Levite families, descended from Merari, received towns from Zebulun. It shows the last group was also cared for.
entries.21:35: Jokneam, Kartah, Dimnah, and Nahalal were given with their pasture land, making four towns. It means their provision was specific and counted.
entries.21:36: From Reuben's tribe they received Bezer and Jahaz with their pasture land. It shows the support came from tribes on the eastern side too.
entries.21:37: Kedemoth and Mephaath were added, making four towns from Reuben. It means the record kept track of every town given.
entries.21:38: From Gad's tribe they received Ramoth in Gilead, a city of refuge, and Mahanaim, with their pasture land. It means they were given a place of safety east of the Jordan as well.
entries.21:39: Heshbon and Jazer were also given, making four towns from Gad. It shows the final towns in this group were carefully listed.
entries.21:40: All these towns went to the Merarite families, the last group of Levites, totaling twelve towns. It means every Levite family received its promised share, and the whole plan was completed.
entries.21:41: The Levites, who served as priests, were given forty-eight towns spread throughout Israel's territory. This shows God made sure those who served him had places to live among the people.
entries.21:42: Each of those towns came with surrounding pasture land for their animals. God's provision included the practical details of daily life, not just the town itself.
entries.21:43: God gave Israel the land he had promised to their ancestors long before. What God promises, he eventually delivers, and the people could settle there as their own.
entries.21:44: God gave the people rest from their enemies on every side, just as he had promised. When God promises peace and safety, he is able to make it happen.
entries.21:45: Not one of God's good promises to Israel failed; every single one came true. You can trust that God keeps his word, even when the wait has been long.
entries.22:1: Joshua called together the tribes that had settled east of the Jordan River. This sets up his farewell to soldiers who had helped the other tribes fight.
entries.22:2: Joshua reminded them that they had obeyed Moses and followed every command he had given them. Their faithfulness is being recognized before they go home.
entries.22:3: For a long time they had stayed with their fellow Israelites and kept serving the Lord. They did not abandon their duty even though their own land was waiting for them.
entries.22:4: Now that the other tribes had peace and safety, these soldiers were free to return to their own land. God had kept his promise of rest, and they could finally go home.
entries.22:5: Joshua urged them to keep loving and obeying God with their whole heart and life. Staying faithful to God matters more than anything else as they begin their new life.
entries.22:6: Joshua blessed them and sent them home. A blessing like this was a prayer for God's good favor to go with them.
entries.22:7: One half of the tribe of Manasseh had already received land east of the Jordan, while the other half got land west with the rest of Israel. Joshua blessed both groups as they parted.
entries.22:8: Joshua told them to go home rich with livestock, metals, and clothing, and to share what they had won with those who had stayed behind. Those who fought should not forget those who supported them.
entries.22:9: The eastern tribes left the gathering place at Shiloh and traveled back to their own land of Gilead. They went as God had directed through Moses.
entries.22:10: When they reached the Jordan River area, they built a large, visible altar. This act would soon cause a serious misunderstanding.
entries.22:11: Word quickly spread that the eastern tribes had built an altar on Israel's side of the river. The other tribes saw this as a possible act of rebellion against God.
entries.22:12: The whole community gathered at Shiloh ready to go to war against them. They took the threat of false worship very seriously.
entries.22:13: Before attacking, Israel sent Phinehas the priest to talk with the eastern tribes. They chose a respected spiritual leader to handle the matter.
entries.22:14: Ten leaders, one from each tribe, went with Phinehas. This showed the whole nation was represented in the confrontation.
entries.22:15: The delegation arrived in Gilead and spoke directly to the eastern tribes. They came to ask questions, not to fight right away.
entries.22:16: The leaders accused them of turning away from God by building their own altar. They believed this was a serious sin against the Lord.
entries.22:17: They reminded them of the disaster at Baal-peor, a past sin that still had consequences. They warned that history could repeat itself.
entries.22:18: They feared that if these tribes turned from God, his anger would fall on the whole nation. One group's sin could bring trouble on everyone.
entries.22:19: They offered a solution: if their land felt unfit for worship, they could move into the Lord's land with the rest of Israel. They begged them not to build a rival altar.
entries.22:20: They pointed to Achan, whose sin brought trouble on all Israel and cost him his life. This showed how one person's wrong can affect many.
entries.22:21: The eastern tribes answered the leaders directly. They were ready to explain their side of the story.
entries.22:22: They called on God himself as witness that they were innocent. They invited God to judge them if they had acted out of pride or sin.
entries.22:23: They declared that if they had built the altar for sacrifices, they deserved to die. They were not hiding anything and accepted God's judgment.
entries.22:24: They explained their real reason: they feared that future generations would be told they had no share in the Lord. They acted out of concern, not rebellion.
entries.22:25: They worried that the Jordan River would be used to separate them from God's people. They feared their children would be pushed away from worshiping the Lord.
entries.22:26: So they decided to build an altar, but not for sacrifices. It was meant for a different purpose entirely.
entries.22:27: The altar was to be a witness between the tribes for future generations. It would prove that the eastern tribes also had the right to worship the Lord.
entries.22:28: They wanted a visible reminder they could point to if anyone questioned their place among God's people. The altar was a copy, a sign, not a place of sacrifice.
entries.22:29: They firmly denied any plan to turn from God or set up a rival altar for offerings. The real altar of the Lord was at his house, and they knew it.
entries.22:30: When Phinehas and the leaders heard this explanation, they were satisfied. The misunderstanding was cleared up peacefully.
entries.22:31: Phinehas said they now knew the Lord was with them because no wrong had been done. The people had been spared from God's judgment.
entries.22:32: Phinehas and the leaders returned to the rest of Israel and reported what they had learned. They brought good news instead of a call to war.
entries.22:33: The people were relieved and praised God. They dropped their plans to attack and destroy the eastern tribes.
entries.22:34: The eastern tribes named the altar "Ed," meaning witness, because it stood as proof that the Lord is God. It reminded everyone of their shared faith.
entries.23:1: After years of peace from their enemies, Joshua had grown very old. It reminds the reader that God's rest is a gift worth remembering as life moves on.
entries.23:2: Joshua gathered Israel's leaders and told them plainly that he was old and near the end of his life. It shows the value of leaders passing on what they have learned before they go.
entries.23:3: Joshua reminded the people that they had seen God fight for them against their enemies. What God has done in the past is reason to trust him now.
entries.23:4: Joshua had already assigned the remaining land to the tribes as their inheritance. It means God's promises are secure even when the work is not yet finished.
entries.23:5: God himself would drive out the remaining nations and give the land to Israel. The reader can rely on God to complete what he has promised.
entries.23:6: Joshua urged the people to be strong and carefully follow everything written in God's law, without drifting off course. Staying faithful to God's word takes deliberate effort.
entries.23:7: They were not to mix with the remaining nations or adopt their gods in any way. The point for the reader is to keep clear of influences that pull you away from God.
entries.23:8: Instead of turning away, they were to stay close to the Lord as they had done so far. Loyalty to God is something to keep up, not just start.
entries.23:9: God had already driven out great and strong nations ahead of them. It shows that no obstacle is too big when God is the one clearing the way.
entries.23:10: One Israelite could chase a thousand enemies because God was fighting for them. The reader is reminded that real strength comes from God, not numbers.
entries.23:11: Joshua told them to watch themselves carefully and keep loving the Lord. Loving God is something you guard and nurture, not something you take for granted.
entries.23:12: If they turned back and joined themselves to the remaining nations through marriage and close ties, trouble would follow. It warns the reader that small compromises can lead you away from God.
entries.23:13: God would then stop driving out those nations, and they would become traps, whips, and thorns to Israel until they lost the land. Disobedience brings real harm, not just a slap on the wrist.
entries.23:14: Joshua said he was about to die, and he reminded them that every good thing God promised had come true. It encourages the reader to trust God's record of keeping his word.
entries.23:15: Just as God kept every good promise, he would also bring the promised judgment if they turned away. God is faithful in both blessing and warning.
entries.23:16: If they broke their agreement with God and served other gods, his anger would burn against them and they would quickly lose the land. It is a serious warning that turning from God has serious consequences.
entries.24:1: Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel and their leaders to stand before God at Shechem. This shows that what he was about to say was serious and meant for everyone, not just the leaders.
entries.24:2: Joshua reminded the people that their ancestors, including Abraham's family, once lived across the river and worshiped other gods. It shows that following the true God was a choice their family had not always made.
entries.24:3: God says he personally took Abraham from that other land, led him through Canaan, and gave him many descendants, starting with Isaac. The point is that God started their whole story and kept his promises.
entries.24:4: God gave Isaac's sons Jacob and Esau their places, with Esau settling in the hill country and Jacob's family later going down to Egypt. This reminds the people how God guided each branch of the family.
entries.24:5: God sent Moses and Aaron and struck Egypt with miraculous signs, then brought the people out. The rescue from Egypt was God's work, not something the people did for themselves.
entries.24:6: When the people left Egypt and reached the Red Sea, the Egyptian army chased them with chariots and horsemen. They were trapped and in real danger.
entries.24:7: When the people cried out, God put darkness between them and the Egyptians and drowned the Egyptian army in the sea. The people saw it with their own eyes, then lived in the desert for a long time.
entries.24:8: God brought them into the land of the Amorites east of the Jordan, and when those people fought them, God gave Israel the victory and the land. God is describing himself as the one who fought for them.
entries.24:9: Balak, the king of Moab, went to war against Israel and hired Balaam to curse them. Cursing meant asking harm to come on them through spiritual power.
entries.24:10: God refused to listen to Balaam's curses and made him bless Israel instead, keeping them safe. God protected his people even when someone was paid to harm them.
entries.24:11: Israel crossed the Jordan and faced Jericho and many other peoples in battle, and God gave them all into Israel's hands. The victories were credited to God, not to Israel's own strength.
entries.24:12: God says he sent a hornet ahead of them to drive out the two Amorite kings, without Israel's swords or bows. The point is that God cleared the way himself.
entries.24:13: God gave them land they had not farmed, towns they had not built, and vineyards and olive groves they had not planted. They were enjoying good things they had received as a gift.
entries.24:14: Joshua tells the people to honor God and serve him sincerely, and to throw out the gods their ancestors had worshiped in the old country and in Egypt. Serving God means a real change of loyalty, not just words.
entries.24:15: Joshua puts the choice plainly: serve the old gods, serve the gods of the land, or serve the Lord, and he states that he and his family will serve the Lord. Each person has to decide whom they will follow.
entries.24:16: The people answered that they would never abandon the Lord to serve other gods. They were rejecting the idea of turning away from the God who had helped them.
entries.24:17: They recalled that the Lord brought them and their ancestors out of slavery in Egypt, did great signs, and kept them safe on all their travels. Their loyalty was based on what God had actually done for them.
entries.24:18: They said the Lord drove out the peoples living in the land, so they would serve him because he is their God. They were committing themselves based on God's help in taking the land.
entries.24:19: Joshua warns them that serving the Lord is not easy, because God is holy and will not share honor with other gods, and he will not overlook their wrongs. He is testing whether they really mean their promise.
entries.24:20: Joshua says that if they turn away and serve foreign gods, God will turn against them and bring them harm after all the good he has done. Loyalty to God is not something to promise lightly.
entries.24:21: The people insisted again that they would serve the Lord. They were standing by their commitment despite Joshua's warning.
entries.24:22: Joshua told them their own words were now witnesses against them, and they agreed. They were accepting that they would be held to what they had promised.
entries.24:23: Joshua told them to get rid of the foreign gods among them and give their hearts fully to the Lord, the God of Israel. The promise had to show up in action, not just in words.
entries.24:24: The people said they would serve the Lord their God and listen to his voice. They were promising both loyalty and obedience.
entries.24:25: Joshua made a formal agreement with the people that day and gave them rules and laws at Shechem. This put their promise into a binding, public commitment.
entries.24:26: Joshua wrote these words in the book of God's law and set up a large stone under the oak tree at the Lord's holy place. The stone was a lasting physical reminder of the agreement.
entries.24:27: Joshua said the stone would be a witness, because all the Lord's words had been spoken in its presence, and it would testify against them if they broke faith with God. It was a visible reminder that they had made a promise.
entries.24:28: Joshua sent the people home, each to their own family land. The gathering ended with everyone returning to their inheritance.
entries.24:29: After these events, Joshua, the servant of the Lord, died at the age of 110. His long life and death marked the end of an era for Israel.
entries.24:30: They buried Joshua in his own land at Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash. He was buried in the inheritance he had been given.
entries.24:31: Israel stayed faithful to the Lord during Joshua's lifetime and during the lives of the older leaders who outlived him and had seen what God did for Israel. Faithfulness continued as long as those who had witnessed God's works were still alive.
entries.24:32: The bones of Joseph, which Israel had carried up from Egypt, were buried at Shechem on land Jacob had bought, which became the inheritance of Joseph's descendants. This fulfilled Joseph's earlier request and closed a long chapter of promise.
entries.24:33: Eleazar, the son of Aaron, died and was buried in the hill country of Ephraim on land given to his son Phinehas. The passing of these leaders marked the end of the generation that had entered the land.
